 Latest news Scammers never miss an opportunity to try to steal people’s money and personal information. Here’s what to watch out for with the 2027 Social Security COLA.
 Kevin Dietsch Social Security Social Security scam alert: How fraudsters are using the 2027 COLA increase to target beneficiaries
 Greg Heilman Update: Oct 24th, 2026 06:17 EDT Share Make us preferred on Google The Social Security Administration has announced a 3.6% boost to benefits in 2027 through the annual cost-of-living adjustment (COLA). This increase is automatically applied but scammers are using the occasion to try to swindle beneficiaries. 
 The SSA put out a warning ahead of the 2027 COLA saying, “don’t pay for promises of increased SSA benefits.” 
 Keep an eye out for these Social Security COLA scams 
 Typically, scammers will contact you via an unsolicited advertisement, email, phone, text or social media messge claiming to be able to “boost,” “unlock,” or “maximize” a person’s Social Security benefit for an upfront fee, says the SSA.
 Remember that the COLA increase is automatically applied to benefits , so Social Security beneficiaries do not need to do anything and this brings us to the first red flag.
 Anyone who contacts you telling you that you must apply for the COLA increase, is a scammer. You will often be told to go to a website and open up a link.
 “If you receive a suspicious message, do not click on any links or attachments,” the SSA has previously warned.
 You should know that the SSA may contact you by email to provide you with information or follow up on an in-person meeting. Phone calls are typically for business purposes such as that you recently applied for benefits, are receiving payments and your record needs to be updated or you have requested a phone call.
 “If there is a problem with your Social Security number or record, we will typically mail you a letter,” states the SSA . Representatives will never make threats or arrest or legal action nor suspension of your Social Security number, demand payment or ask for personal details or banking information .
 Anyone asking you to send payment via gift card, pre-paid debit card, internet currency, or mail or wire cash, is not with the SSA. 
 In a prior scam alert notice from the SSA, the agency advises people who receive suspicious communications: “ Do not take immediate action. If you receive a communication that causes a strong emotional response, take a deep breath. Hang up or ignore the message. Talk to someone you trust.”
 The agency also says to “be skeptical” as “scammers can create fake numbers and identities. Do not trust your caller ID.” 
 Likewise, if you are contacted by someone claiming to be from the government or law enforcement informing you of a problem that you do not recognize or an unsolicited offer “do not provide your personal information, even if the caller has some of your information.” 
 In a Better Business Bureau (BBB) warning of red flags they recommend that “when in doubt, hang up.” It’s better to be safe than sorry if you think you may be getting scammed. You can confirm that the correspondence is legitimate by calling the SSA at 1-800-772-1213 or visiting the agency’s webpage SSA.gov .
 What do I do if I get scammed? 
 If you believe that you are the victim of fraud the Federal Trade Commission asks that you report it to them at ReportFraud.ftc.gov .
